summary: Teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus frees a woman who has been bent over for eighteen years, and answers the indignant synagogue ruler.
key_insight: Jesus answers the ruler with a picture of untying. Every farmer would “loose” his ox or donkey on the Sabbath to lead it to water; this daughter of Abraham, “whom Satan has bound,” must be “loosed” too. If an animal may be untied for a drink, how much more a woman bound for eighteen years.
story: Jesus was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. A woman was there who had had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not straighten herself at all.
When Jesus saw her, He called her to Him and said, “Woman, you are loosed from your infirmity.” He laid His hands on her, and immediately she stood up straight and glorified God.

But the ruler of the synagogue was indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath. He turned to the crowd and said, “There are six days on which men ought to work; therefore come and be healed on them, and not on the Sabbath day.”

The Lord answered him, “Hypocrite! Does not each one of you on the Sabbath loose his ox or donkey from the stall, and lead it away to water it? So ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound, think of it, for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath?”
When He said these things, all His adversaries were put to shame, and the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things He was doing.

scene.label: A spirit of infirmity
scene.text: Luke, “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), describes her condition with care: bent double and unable to straighten. He also says a spirit lay behind it, and Jesus says Satan had bound her. Yet Jesus does not cast out a spirit here; He speaks a word of release and lays His hands on her.

scene.label: Six days
scene.text: The ruler was quoting the commandment, “Six days you shall labor” (Exodus 20:9). In his eyes healing was work, and a woman who had waited eighteen years could wait one more day.

scene.label: Animals on the Sabbath
scene.text: The Sabbath gave rest to ox and donkey as well as people (Deuteronomy 5:14), but no farmer let his animals go thirsty. Later Jewish writings confirm that an animal could be led out to water on the Sabbath. Jesus argues from what His critics already did every week.

scene.label: Daughter of Abraham
scene.text: The phrase appears nowhere else in Scripture. Jesus gives a bent, overlooked woman a title of full belonging in God’s covenant people, as He will later call Zacchaeus “a son of Abraham” (Luke 19:9).

witnesses.luke: Only Luke tells this healing, and it is the last time his Gospel shows Jesus teaching in a synagogue. It stands with two other Sabbath disputes over healing that Luke records (6:6–11; 14:1–6) and with his care for women others overlooked, from the widow of Nain to the women who traveled with Jesus. Luke ends it, as he likes to, with the crowd rejoicing.

seeing.reveals: Jesus sees the woman before she asks, calls her to Himself, and frees her with a word and a touch. He came to loose what Satan has bound, and He will not make her wait for a more convenient day.
seeing.living: The Sabbath, and every gathering of God’s people, is meant for setting people free, not for guarding rules against them. Look for the person in the room who has been bent low for years and cannot lift her head, and bring her to Jesus rather than to a rule.
seeing.ponder: What has kept you bent over for years, and will you let Jesus call you to Him today?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus came to free those Satan has bound, and the Sabbath is the right day for it.
preaching.watch_for: The ruler says there are six days on which men “ought” to work (v. 14). Jesus answers with His own “ought” (v. 16): this woman ought to be set free on the Sabbath, of all days.
